title: KV warmth signatures and eviction heuristics - field notes
body:
Purpose and framing:

These are field notes from a set of exploratory experiments we ran to better understand "warmth" (temporal locality) signatures in the KV cache and how different eviction heuristics and light-weight prefetch policies interact with paging and memory bandwidth on our T4/P4 fleet. The goal: identify robust, low-risk knobs we can flip in the runtime to reduce tail latency under heavy multi-tenant workloads without large memory overhead.

Summary of findings (high-level):
- Warm prefixes are concentrated: ~12% of unique KV keys account for ~72% of cache hits for our 1k-5k token prefix lengths on chat workloads.
- Simple recency-based eviction (LRU) performs well at low to moderate occupancy but degrades quickly when page-thrashing occurs at >85% resident set for model KV arrays.
- Introducing a tiny frequency multiplier (decayed LFU hybrid) recovered ~9–12% tail latency at high cache pressure with negligible extra memory for counters (1 byte per 256 keys via sampling).
- Aggressive prefetching reduces average token latency in stable workloads but substantially increases memory bandwidth and paging when input sequence diversity increases; hit improvement came at the cost of increased stall time under realistic noise.

Experiment matrix and knobs tested:
- Workloads: 3 synthetic mixes + 2 replayed traces from production chat (one consumer app, one support chatbot).
- Cache sizes: 30%, 50%, 70%, 90% of observed working set (measured via offline trace).
- Eviction policies: pure LRU, CLOCK-probation hybrid, decayed LFU (exponential decay tau=30s / 300s), and MRU for comparison.
- Prefetch policies: none, next-token-only prefetch, predictive-prefetch (simple n-gram from traces), and multi-prefetch (k=4).
- Sampling granularity: full-key counters, 1:16 sampled counters, and 1:256 approximate counters.

Instrumentation and profiling notes:
- Tools used: per-request timeline from tracing agent, nvprof for kernel-level memory traffic (aggregated), and an in-process microprofiling hook that recorded: cache lookup time, eviction time, page fault counts, and kv-transfer bytes.
- Key metrics captured: hit rate, reuse interval distribution, average eviction latency, page fault/sec (majors+minors), PCIe DMA utilization, and CPU cycles in eviction path.
- Important caveats: nvprof on P4 nodes undercounts small DMA ops; use aggregated PCIe bus counters from host as sanity. Also, microprofile adds ~0.8% overhead in fast paths — accounted for in baseline runs.

Representative results (selected; numbers are median over 5 runs unless noted):
- Production-chat-trace-A (high reuse): 50% cache size
  - LRU: hit 61%, avg token latency 21ms, tail 99p 72ms, page faults 14/s
  - Decayed-LFU (tau=30s, sampled 1:64): hit 69%, avg 18.3ms (-12.8%), tail 99p 62ms (-13.9%), page faults 11/s
  - Prefetch next-token: hit 72% but avg 19.7ms (prefetch cost + bandwidth), tail 99p 85ms (worse)

- Mixed-synth-high-diversity: 70% cache size
  - LRU: hit 44%, avg 28ms, tail 99p 150ms, major page faults 28/s
  - CLOCK-probation: hit 48%, avg 25ms, tail 99p 110ms
  - LFU-sampled: hit 50%, avg 23.5ms, tail 99p 95ms, but PCIe utilization increased 18% vs LRU (prefetch not used)
body_continue:
Eviction micro-behavior and warmness signatures:
1) Reuse interval modes: There are two dominant reuse regimes: tight reuse (<1s) representing interactive follow-on tokens in a session, and long-tail reuse (10s-10m) mostly from background redistribution and repeated prompts. These map to distinct key sizes and alignment patterns in KV shards.
2) Cold-to-warm ramp: Keys crossing a small activity threshold (3 hits within 8s) are disproportionately likely to be re-accessed in the next 30s. That suggests an inexpensive heuristic: promote on thin repeated access instead of waiting for long-term LFU signals.
3) Eviction churn: Under LRU and high occupancy, eviction churn correlates strongly with increased minor page faults and DMA reclaims — suggests eviction path touches cold pages that have been paged-out, causing extra I/O.

Prefetch tradeoffs and memory bandwidth behavior:
- Predictive prefetch (n-gram) helps when traces have very repetitive next-token patterns (e.g., multi-turn assistant where utterances follow templates). But in diverse user-generated inputs, prefetch adds noise: additional KV reads that displace warm items while adding memory bandwidth (measured +25–40% PCIe traffic).
- Next-token lightweight prefetch performed OK only when constrained to a small speculative budget (<= 1% of cache footprint) and when combined with a probation region that protects recently used keys from displacement.

Operational suggestions (low-to-medium risk):
- Implement a "thin-promote" heuristic: promote keys to protected set after N hits within T seconds (suggest N=3, T=8s). This yields much of LFU benefit without counters.
- Replace full 8-byte counters with sampled 1-byte counters at 1:64 sampling for LFU-style weight; storage cost <2% and gives good discrimination.
- Add a small probation/pinned bucket (<= 6% of cache) that is populated by thin-promote and only demoted by explicit demotion policy so short bursts don't get evicted.
- Disable aggressive predictive prefetch by default; expose a flag for tenant/route opt-in and restrict prefetch budget and a prefetch-probation circuit breaker that shrinks budget when page-faults or PCIe utilization exceed thresholds.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- How sensitive are the thin-promote thresholds to very short sessions (mobile clients) vs long sessions (server-batched)? We need AB runs across two real tenant groups (SRV-2245).
- Could we leverage model-side signals (e.g., KV access patterns during generation) to better prioritize prefetch decisions? This requires light-weight cross-component telemetry and will need an RFC.
- Is there value in a tiny in-memory bloom-filter style "recently-accessed" sketch that survives evictions to reduce re-warm cost? Prototypeable but adds complexity.

Next steps and experiment plan (concrete):
- Implement thin-promote + probation bucket in a feature branch (PR linked). Start with defaults N=3,T=8s, probation cap 6%. Run controlled canaries on dedicated nodes with production-chat-trace-A replay for 48h.
- Add sampled 1-byte counter path as an opt-in config; benchmark memory overhead and discrimination on the mixed-synth traces.
- Build lightweight prefetch circuit-breaker metric (PCIe util and minor page faults) and gate predictive prefetch behind it.

Notes to reviewers:
- See PR for implementation details and microbench harness (PR link in linked_artifacts). The field runs used realistic co-tenancy: two other tenant traffic patterns were replayed at 0.5x and 0.2x scale.
- I deliberately kept instrumentation coarse to avoid perturbing behavior; fine-grained per-key histograms are available in the raw logs if needed.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets used during profiling:
- host-level PCIe aggregated counters: sudo nvidia-smi nvlink --query-gpu=pcie_throughput --format=csv
- eviction path flamegraph: ./scripts/eviction-flame.sh --trace=run1234 > flame.svg
- basic trace replay harness: python tools/replay.py --trace traces/prod-chat-A.json --rate 1.0 --scale 1.0 --target http://localhost:8080/generate

Rough action items:
- [ ] Kick off canary with thin-promote in next week (owner: Miguel)
- [ ] Add sampled-counter opt-in and run memory regression (owner: Evelyn)
- [ ] Prepare an AB template for product team to opt routes into prefetch (owner: Tom)

If folks want, I can merge the raw run logs into the shared bucket and run a short visualization pass (reuse-interval CDFs, eviction traces). Not final — just field notes, welcome critique and experiments to prioritize.
